units.title: Yellow warning: wind
units.author: met
units.text: Marrow Sound, issued 05:30 ST. Yellow warning for wind in force from 06:00 until 23:00. Southwest gale 8, gusting 50 knots on exposed coasts and islands, veering west later. Heavy rain this morning, then squally showers. Sea rough or very rough, with a long swell of 2.5 to 3.5 m on south and east facing shores. Max 10 C. Tomorrow: wind decreasing 4 or 5, sea moderate, swell slowly easing.

units.author: ferry
units.text: Sound Lines. Due to the gale, all sailings to Lisle and Gilliver are suspended this morning; we will review at 12:00. Our relief vessel remains in the basin at Weyhaven and will not move until the wind eases. There is no change to our position on Kittering Holm: we will help with a daylight transfer when it is judged safe. No sailing is scheduled.

units.author: coast
units.text: Coastguard Marrow Sound. A small craft warning is in force for the whole Sound today. Do not put to sea. Regarding Kittering Holm: planning continues for a vessel-based transfer in daylight, at the earliest once the swell at the east dock has fallen below safe limits. A provisional window at first light later this week is being assessed against the forecast. It is not confirmed.

units.title: Gilliver and Lisle: supply interruption
units.author: power
units.text: Sound Power Co-op. Around 380 properties in Gilliver and parts of Lisle lost supply at 08:12 when conductors clashed in the gale on the coast road. Crews are on site. We expect most customers to be restored by early afternoon. If you rely on powered medical equipment and have not registered with us, please call now. Treat any fallen line as live.

units.author: power
units.text: Update 14:20. Supply has been restored to all affected properties in Gilliver and Lisle. Thank you for your patience. A small number of customers on the Gilliver harbour front may notice brief flickers this evening while we complete repairs on the coast road. These are planned and are not a new fault.

units.title: Gale closes the Sound; Holm plans on hold
units.author: soundfm
units.text: 08:30 ST. All ferries are off and there's a small craft warning across the Sound. The Coastguard says the gale doesn't change its plans for Kittering Holm, it just pushes them back. The swell at the island's east dock is put at around three metres this morning, well beyond what any landing could manage.

units.title: 'I just want someone to tell him I'm fine'
units.author: weypost
units.text: A Weyhaven woman whose younger brother is believed to have been working on Kittering Holm when the clearance contract ended says she has had no information from his employer. She asked not to be named. 'I'm not angry yet,' she said. 'I just want someone to tell him I'm fine, so he stops worrying about me.'

units.author: weypost
units.text: She said her brother had taken the job for the money and to prove he could, and had written to her in batches whenever the supply boat ran. 'He saves them up and sends them all at once,' she said. 'The last lot were about a dog and a truck. He loves a truck.'

units.author: weypost
units.text: Grieve Land Services did not respond to the Post's questions about how families of site staff are being kept informed. The Coastguard said families could call its public line, but that it could not share personal details over the telephone and did not hold a list of names it could confirm.

units.title: Analysis: who is responsible when a contractor walks?
units.author: tradejournal
units.text: The Kittering Holm case has prompted questions across the land-services sector about what happens to site staff when a contract ends early on a remote site. Most standard forms place responsibility for 'safe demobilisation' on the principal contractor, but leave the details to site plans that are rarely published.

units.author: tradejournal
units.text: One operations director, who asked not to be named, said remote island work is normally priced with a 'standby vessel' clause. 'If that clause was struck out to save money, somebody signed that off,' she said. Grieve has not said whether its contract with Ardent Vale included such a clause.

units.author: tradejournal
units.text: Industry veterans also recalled an earlier northern contract that ended abruptly, though none would give details on the record. 'There's always one job people don't talk about,' said a retired site manager. 'Usually it's because it was badly run, not because of anything else.'

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 14:30 ST. Power is back in Gilliver after a morning outage. At the village hall, volunteers kept the urn going off a camping stove. One told us: 'People keep coming in to ask, and then they stay, because nobody wants to be at home on their own listening to the wind.'

units.title: We'd love your feedback!
units.author: camp_supply_news
units.text: Hi there! How was your last Camp Supply order? Tell us in our two-minute survey and you could win a $50 voucher. Plus, this week only: buy any two lanterns and get a set of window hooks free. Hang a light where you can see it! Questions? Our team is here 9 to 5, weekdays. Happy camping!

units.title: Nothing useful
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi. I'm told this email account closes at the end of the week. I've sent the Coastguard everything we hold: dock drawings, the fuel log, the camp plan, the radio frequencies, the crew list as it stood at the start. I keep opening the spreadsheet to check where we are on numbers, out of habit. There aren't any numbers any more. I'm sorry. Ruth

units.title: the wind
units.author: sam
units.text: it's blowing a gale here, the bins went over and the dog barked at them for an hour like they'd personally insulted him. the radio says nothing can go out today and that it doesn't change the plan, it just moves it, which I've decided to find comforting. I made Mum's tea and she asked if you'd remembered your good socks. I said yes. love, S x

units.author: hal_brannock
units.text: Still nothing with a hull the Coastguard will sign off in this weather, chief. The lad who put the phone down rang back and apologised. He worked Corran. He said, word for word, 'they told us the boat was coming too'. Then he said it was a different job and a different firm's boat, and to forget it. I'm telling you because you'd want to know, not because it means anything.

units.title: Sorry, me again
units.author: ana_reyner
units.text: Sorry, me again. The wind is so loud here I keep thinking it must be worse where he is. I went to his flat and watered the plant and did his washing up, which he'll pretend to be annoyed about. If you see him, tell him I'm fine. Tell him I'm not watching the news, even though I am, all the time. Ana

units.title: Second lamp
units.author: morrow_unknown
units.text: Sorry if this is strange. The power went off here this morning in the gale, and when it came back the woman next door put a second lamp in her window, the one facing the water. Then the house beside hers did. By ten tonight the whole front had two. Nobody organised it that I know of. I might be reading too much into it. Morrow

units.title: From the archive: a 1953 correction notice
units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: Editor's note: readers asked whether the Courier ever reported people stranded on the Holm. We have found no such report. The nearest is this correction from a 1953 issue, page 2: 'In our report of the 14th we stated that the Lights Board survey party remained on Kittering Holm overnight. We are asked to say that the party returned each evening before dusk, as was their custom.' G. Faulds

units.title: 'Our Gilliver Correspondent', 1902: the window lamps
units.author: courier_1890s
units.text: Visitors to our village sometimes remark upon the lamps kept in the cottage windows of an evening, facing out over the Sound. Your correspondent has asked several of the older wives the reason, and has been told, variously, that it is for the boats, for luck, for the drowned, and 'for manners'. One good lady told him it was none of his business, which he records as the most honest answer.

units.author: oral_history_1970s
units.text: Interviewer: Did anyone ever not keep a lamp? Mr P. (b. 1902): 'The Tregears didn't, after the war. Thought it was nonsense.' [laughs] 'Nothing happened to them. Nothing at all. They just moved to Ammet.' [long pause] 'Mind, they moved in the middle of the winter, which nobody does, with the roads how they were.'

units.title: Talk: Holm timber camp (1894-95)
units.author: hist_wiki_pell
units.text: Talk note. The claim that the camp was abandoned 'because of something the men saw' is poorly sourced: it appears first in a 1960s tourist pamphlet. The Courier's own 1895 column says only that the men were 'in poor spirits'. I argued earlier for a pay dispute; the wage ledger shows full pay, so I have withdrawn that. That leaves the frost, which is the dullest explanation and therefore my favourite. Pell

units.author: camp_clerk_1894
units.text: Decr. 21st. Shortest day. 12 trees. Roll at dusk, 17 men, three having gone over on the fish boat with no leave and no pay drawn, which I enter against them though I do not blame them. Coad has had the lamps set in a ring round the bunk huts. He will not say what for. I asked was it for the deer and he laughed, there being no deer on this island.

units.author: fisher_diary_1930s
units.text: Jan. 6. Calm and bitter. Jory wont go out. Says he'll go any day but not this one and not to the Holm side, and wouldnt say why, him that never refused a day in his life. I went alone and hauled the near pots. Fair catch, sold at 1s 4d. When I come in Jory had the lamp lit already and was sat by it like a dog by a door.

units.author: carrow_keeper
units.text: Feb. 2. 00:00 wind W 2, clear, hard frost. 02:00 calm, vis. very good, lamp burning well. Remarks: none on the shore road. Rowe says it is the first quiet night this month and he slept. I note he has asked the Board, by letter of the 30th, to be moved to a rock station, 'anywhere with no road to it'. Forwarded. E.S.

units.author: wx_carrowpoint
units.text: Overnight minimum 996 hPa at 04:10, gusts to 47 knots at the station, and my anemometer cup is now somewhere in a field. Swell at the point 3.2 m at dawn. Rain 22 mm since midnight. This is the worst of it if the charts are right, and after tonight it should fall away quickly. I'll be up at five tomorrow for the swell reading.

units.author: sb_bins
units.text: The gale took Rope Walk's bins down to the harbour wall, where they now sit in a row like a queue for a bus that isn't coming. The council will no doubt say collections are 'running as normal'. I have rung. A woman told me they are 'prioritising the coast road' and I said the coast road does not pay my council tax. Bernard (Rope Walk)

units.author: retired_teacher
units.text: I taught two of the ferry crew who have put their names down for the relief sailing, and I said last week that they are not people who make things up. I would add that they are not people who volunteer for nothing, either. Whatever is or isn't on that island, somebody thought it worth asking for a boat. I'd ask posters to keep that in mind, and to spell 'Coastguard' as one word.

units.author: skeptic_ferrous
units.text: Gil, I did read it back, and you're right that you didn't say 'on purpose'. My apology. But the list is still telling you two incompatible stories and you're passing on both. The only facts I can find are a beacon, an acknowledged alert, camp lights seen every night, and a company that won't say who it left. That's enough to worry about without inventing anything.

units.author: truthwatch_gil

edit.note: edited: source withdrew the timer claim
edit.text: Accepted, thank you. I've taken out what I wrote here about the lights being on solar timers: my source now says they 'may have been thinking of a different site'. Fine. I'm leaving the question, though, and I'll keep asking it: why won't Grieve say how many people it left out there?

units.text: Accepted, thank you. New information though: a source says the lights Bram sees are on solar timers, Grieve leaves them on at all its sites so nobody nicks the plant. So the lights prove nothing about anybody being there. Do your research.

units.author: propwatch_ledger
units.text: Finding 2, checked twice: the intermediary's dock notice lists the Holm pier as 'temporary, for the duration of works'. If the works have ended, I don't know who now holds the right to land there. I've written to the council planning office and to the intermediary. Finding 3: nothing. I'm out of findings, and for once I'm glad to say so.

units.author: sb_mod
units.text: Added for the list. Coastguard: small craft warning today, and 'a provisional window at first light later this week is being assessed against the forecast. It is not confirmed.' Sound Lines: no sailing scheduled, relief vessel still in the basin. Sound Power: Gilliver and Lisle supply restored at 14:20. Pell.

units.author: gilliver_lamp
units.text: Mrs Hale is right. Most of the front put a second lamp in after the power came back this morning. I did not ask anyone to and nor did anyone ask me. My neighbour's boy carried a spare up the hill to old Mr Pask, who cannot manage the stairs any more. Maud

units.author: sb_commuter_lisle
units.text: Ferries off all day, so I worked from my mother's kitchen table on Lisle and listened to it blow. One thing for the list that isn't a rumour: the Sound Lines desk told me on the phone that their volunteer list for the relief sailing is 'longer than the boat'. They didn't need to tell me that. I think they wanted somebody to know.

units.author: wx_carrowpoint
units.text: Evening summary. Wind veered west and dropping, 24 knots now from 41 at noon. Pressure rising fast, 1004 and climbing. Swell still 2.9 m, but the period's shortening, which is what you want. Tomorrow should be a big improvement. Found the anemometer cup in Mrs Tull's hedge; thank you to whoever rang.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Timers don't walk about. Before the gale came in last night one of the lights went from the yard to the cabin end and back, slow, like someone carrying it. I'm not saying more than that. Couldn't go out today, nobody could. I'll look again tonight if it clears.

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: So it's a lamp on a timer or a bloke with a torch, and either way he's fine. Half of you are writing these lads off and the other half are writing a horror film. Sit tight, they'll be picked up and on the telly by the weekend, moaning about the food.

units.title: Found: black and white collie, Gilliver coast road
units.author: gilliver_teen
units.text: found a black and white collie on the coast road by the bus shelter at about 9, no collar, soaked, v friendly. she's out the back of the chippy with a towel and a sausage. not a joke, I know my record on here. if she's yours message the chippy or come and get her.

units.author: morrow_unknown
units.text: Sorry to come in on this. I'm on the Gilliver front most nights on the way to work. The lights on the Holm are not all at the same height and they don't all come on together, which isn't how I'd expect timers to behave. I might be wrong, I'm not a lights person. I just didn't want the timer idea to go unchallenged.

units.author: harbourmaster_quill
units.text: Thank you, Bram. I have passed the point about the ramp drying at half tide to the Coastguard in writing, so it doesn't rely on anybody's notebook. For everyone's information, under byelaw 22 the harbour is closed to all departures until the small craft warning is lifted. Please check your moorings tonight. HM

units.author: ferry_engineer_seth
units.text: Update: she floated this morning in the basin and the yard tied her straight back up when the gusts hit 45. Shaft is quiet, gearbox is quiet, that's two less things for me to swear at. Floodlights are wired. If the wind drops like the charts say, sea trials tomorrow afternoon, and I'll be the one listening to her bearings.

units.author: ferry_mate_kerris
units.text: Good. Briefing for the volunteers tomorrow at the terminal, the company says, weather permitting, which is the phrase of the week. Odell's going to skipper if it happens. I'll be on the bow with the lines. I'm repeating myself but I'll say it: daylight only, and nobody gets left on that pier.

units.author: deckhand_finn
units.text: Not going to talk about the other thing so don't ask. I'm on a fishing boat now. My skipper offered the boat to the Coastguard for daylight and they said thanks but too small. Good. I'd have gone. I'd rather not have. That's all I'm putting on here.

units.title: Coast road fault this morning
units.author: lineman_tess
units.text: Was on the coast road job this morning, my last call-out before I move to days. Two conductors clashed in the gale at the pole by the bus shelter, simple as that, burn marks and all, no mystery. Restored by two. Gilliver front was dark for six hours and I counted lamps in the windows driving past in the van. Every house. I've never seen that.

units.title: Forecourt report
units.author: lh_convenience_kestrel
units.text: Forecourt report. The man at the edge of the light was back at ten past midnight. New coat again. I went out with a coffee because I'm a fool. He took it, said 'thank you, my lift's late', and got into a car four minutes later. So. That's that. I'm a little disappointed, which I think says more about me than him.

units.author: lh_student_kestrel
units.text: taro this is the most wholesome thing on this forum and I'm counting it as a win for humanity. update from the lab: chapter four is with my supervisor, the corridor lights are behaving, I've had nine coffees and no thoughts. it's raining so hard the roof sounds like applause. going to sleep under the desk like a professional.

units.title: From the gallery, tonight
units.author: lh_lighttender_tamsin
units.text: The wind came round to the north this evening and brought a thin rain that the beam turns into a moving wall. I kept the gallery door shut, as I said I would. At ten to one I looked down anyway, and there was a walker on the cliff path, just where the light stops, as there sometimes is. I raised a hand. I always do. I didn't wait to see if it raised one back.

units.title: Utilities helpline, part three hundred
units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: Helpline update. Tonight's hits: a man who wanted to know if the moon affects his meter (no), a woman who read me her entire bill (lovely voice), and the autodialler, which is back, at 02:14, same as before. Script says I must say 'thank you for calling' to the autodialler. I do. It never thanks me back. Rude.

units.title: Break-room notes
units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: Break-room notes. Ward 9 is full of coughs and grumbles, the usual November. The intercom has not said anybody's name since that one time, and I've stopped looking up when it crackles, mostly. The porter here knows someone who knows someone in your Marrow Sound and says they're all lighting lamps. That's a nice thing to do. Back to it.

units.title: End of shift, bus home
units.author: lh_miner_vellmark
units.text: End of shift, on the bus. Pump on level four packed in at two and we had it running by half three, which is the job. Somebody on the crew had seen the news from your Sound about the people on the island. Old Harri said 'they'll keep in the lamp's circle if they've sense'. Then he went back to sleep against the window. Tradition, not belief.

units.author: dc_8_benedikt
units.text: Today I deliver in the Weyhaven docks area. Many customers ask me about the island because my van says 'Sound' on the side, which is only the company name. I tell them I know nothing. It is true. Sorry for spelling. I still do not use the stairs, but I checked and the lights are on.

units.title: Sketch: the stairwell, lit (boring, which is the point)
units.author: dc_14_ivy
units.text: New sketch, described for those without the image: the 6-8 landing, every light on, a fire extinguisher, a crisp packet, someone's bike lock left on the rail (yours? it's still there). Nothing in the corners, for once. I drew it because a friend of a friend is waiting on news from that island and I wanted to draw a place with the lights on.

units.title: Gale ambience, chandlery roof (wind only, honestly)
units.author: hobby_hydrophone
units.text: Took the hydrophone out of the water before the gale and put a contact mic on the chandlery roof instead, with permission from Rook, who asked if I was 'one of those'. Forty minutes of the roof flexing, a loose halyard ringing on the next boat, and the harbour pump cycling every six minutes. Yes, I checked the pump was actually on this time.

units.author: skeptic_hollis
units.text: Quick analysis: the halyard sits at 612 Hz with clean harmonics; the roof flex is broadband under 80 Hz; the pump is a 48 Hz line on six-minute cycles. Textbook. A good recording, and it's nice to have a file in this forum that I can fully explain without a single caveat.

units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: That halyard is a lovely thing at about 22 minutes, almost a bell. I'm staying in on gale nights for the foreseeable, so this is as close as I'll get to one. Thanks for checking the pump, and thanks to Rook for the roof. Make of it what you will.
